STRENGTHS: (1) Real, validated pain point: 34 of 41 interviewed contractors lost a job start date to permit issues, and the founders have firsthand exposure (CEO handled permits at a remodeling firm; urban planning lead interned in a permit office). (2) Early traction with meaningful outcome data: pilot cut first-review rejections from ~38% to ~14% and approval time by ~9 days; 8 of 12 pilots converted to paid (67%), which is strong evidence of willingness to pay at $780/year. (3) Clear positioning: contractor-facing and cross-city, versus single-city tools, city-side portals, and costly expeditors ('hundreds per application'), with a credible price/value gap. (4) Attractive unit economics on paper: software runs locally, low serving cost, >80% projected gross margin, annual license pricing. (5) Capital-efficient: $60K raised, 23 paying customers, ~$19K ARR, a launched site generating leads, and a waitlist indicating demand for more cities. (6) Complementary team, advisors, and a data-feedback concept (rejection patterns) that could become a moat.

WEAKNESSES: (1) Scalability and maintenance risk: the core product depends on integrating with many city portals that have no APIs and change often; supporting 25 metros means hundreds of jurisdictions, and the engineering cost to maintain 'city connections' is likely understated versus the claimed 80% margin. Adding 8 cities with $25K and one summer engineer looks optimistic. (2) Desktop architecture is a strategic liability: hard to learn from users at scale (conflicts with the claimed data moat unless data is sent back), slower iteration, installation/support friction, and the founders themselves question when to go hybrid. The moat claim is internally inconsistent with local-only data storage. (3) Market sizing is naive: '1 in 10 firms paying' top-down math, and the stated target (1,500 firms) vs. break-even at ~450 customers needs a credible acquisition channel; current leads come mainly from the website, and CAC, sales cycle, and churn are not addressed. Forecast jumps (23 to 120 to 600 customers) lack a go-to-market plan. (4) Thin economics at current scale: ~$19K ARR, break-even at ~450 customers (~$350K+ ARR), and a $60K raise gives limited runway; the 12-pilot sample is small and potentially friendly. (5) Dependency and defensibility risks: city portals could block automation or change terms, incumbents (project management software, Procore-type players) or expediting firms could add permit features, and the data moat is unproven. Regulatory/liability exposure if an application filed through the tool is wrong is unaddressed. (6) Team is student-led with limited commercial, sales, and scaling experience; no indication of full-time commitment or a go-to-market hire. (7) Ask is small and focused on a competition prize rather than a scalable funding path.

OVERALL: A well-validated problem with promising early pilot results and good founder-market fit, but significant unresolved risks in technical scalability, architecture, go-to-market, and defensibility. Investment interest is moderate: worth following or a small seed/accelerator-level bet, contingent on evidence of repeatable acquisition, lower per-city maintenance cost, and a web/hybrid architecture that enables the data moat.
